newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts see Roche net rise, debate buyback.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Roche net rise, debate buyback.

text.p: Roche Holding AG is still the favourite in the Swiss pharmaceuticals sector despite fanfare surrounding new rival Novartis AG and now the stock is in the spotlight amid buyback talk and recurrent acquisition rumours.
Roche is due to report 1996 financial data next week. Its annual news conference is scheduled for April 15.
The consensus forecast calls for a 1996 profit rise of some 17.6 percent to 3.97 billion Swiss francs ($2.7 billion) after a 1995 group net profit of 3.37 billion.
The company in January reported that its 1996 sales rose 11 percent to 15.96 billion Swiss francs.
Roche is one of the favourites within the pharma sector.
The group has been producing a solid earnings stream in past years, including a compound profit increase of 15.7 percent in 1994 and 17.8 percent in 1995.
And with some 23 new products in the latter stages of clinical trials, growth is forecast to continue at a similar pace into the foreseeable future.
But aside from strong fundamentals, one central factor behind the Roche allure is a cash pile of some 15 billion francs and speculation about what the company will do with it.

Roche has told analysts it accepts a widely-held view that consolidation in its industry will ultimately mean in future only players with the sheer size and financial strength to control a four to five percent market share will stay on top.
Roche currently has a market share just below three percent.
In recent months rumours have linked Roche to just about every pharmaceuticals company thought to be in play.
But more recently, some analysts are speculating that Roche might instead look to increase shareholder value through a partial buyback of its participation certificates.

Such a move would imply that management believes the certificates are undervalued. It would also reassure investors that 15 to 16 billion Swiss francs are not going to be spent on diversification and return capital to investors for them to reinvest as they choose, Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB) said in a report published this week.
"We think the market would react in a very positive way to a buyback, and we would be applauding loudly," the report said.
Swiss companies tend to shy away from buybacks because of unfavourable tax treatment.

But CSFB analyst Genghis Lloyd-Harris argues that Roche could make a tender offer for certificates and structure the deal in such a way that it would cancel the certificates with no adverse tax consequences for the company or investors.
The topic is particularly timely. The Swiss government is currently in the process of looking at proposals to amend rules governing activities such as buybacks.
CSFB also said a review of the takeover possibilities available to Roche should lead to the conclusion that a buyback is more likely.

"A buyback of GS (participation certificates) is much more likely than a major acquisition since virtually none of the attractive companies in the $5-15 billion price bracket are available, and a $30 plus billion transaction could involve excessive or unwelcome risk," Lloyd-Harris wrote in his report.
CSFB also said it did not believe the probability of a buyback was factored into the current share price.

But a repurchase of this type, even if Roche used all of its available cash, would only have a relatively minor impact on the group's capital structure while robbing it of the ability to act quickly to take advantage of an acquisition opportunity, said Bank Julius Baer analyst Beat Alpiger.
"We've thought about this as a possibility...I have my doubts," Alpiger said.
But he also said a third option for Roche might be some type of change to its capital structure as a prelude to a merger or some other strategic alliance.
($ = 1.454 Swiss Francs)
